Results on Qwen3.5-4B, on which the recipe was developed, and a replication on Olmo-3-7B-Think suggest that the saving depends on how verbose the base model is.

title: DiabAgent: Toward Agentic Physiological Control
summary: As pretraining scales, medical language models have advanced rapidly in clinical question answering. Their ability to achieve effective physiological control through sustained intervention still lacks systematic quantitative evaluation. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting: impaired insulin secretion creates dependence on exogenous insulin, with dosing continually adjusted using information about meals, exercise, illness, and glucose measurements. We introduce DiabAgent, a research suite for agentic physiological control comprising the Agentic Physiological Control (APC) framework, the DiabetSim simulator, and the SweetBench benchmark. APC controls glucose through medical-device tools, using ongoing observations to infer individual states, accumulate personal experience, and choose treatment actions. We build DiabetSim to simulate different patients, events, and device conditions for scalable virtual testing and training. Using DiabetSim, we construct SweetBench by instantiating 32 scenario designs as 212 glucose-control tasks. With Claude Opus 5.5 and a fixed decision interval of one hour, APC achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for the open-source closed-loop baseline OpenAPS. Ablations further show that individual adaptation and contextual information improve glucose control. Combining high-frequency rule-based control with lower-frequency agent decisions shows potential for balancing control performance and computational cost. Our work provides a framework, simulator, and evaluation foundation for agents to participate in human physiological control.

title: Forecasting Earth Surface Change in Embedding Space
summary: Repeated satellite imagery permits understanding of how our planet changes over time, letting us predict its future and plan mitigating actions. Most existing studies that rely on a time series of satellite observations forecast the spectral values at each pixel for a future target date. However, clouds, shadows, and sensor noise often corrupt these observations, so that spectral forecasters waste much of their capacity on low-level features or noise rather than real change. With the advent of Earth foundation models, we argue that forecasting in embedding space is a feasible and more effective alternative. To this end, we design a token space that handles irregular histories from different sensors and foundation models and supports forecasts at any query date. Tokens from this space are inputs to our proposed forecaster, E$^2$Forecast, which is a transformer with two branches: a Gaussian branch that directly predicts a mean point forecast and per-dimension standard deviations, and a rectified-flow branch that generates forecast ensembles. On Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 benchmarks, forecasting embeddings instead of spectral values halves the cosine distance (from 0.20 to 0.10) and greatly reduces overconfidence, lowering the z-score standard deviation from 2.63 to 1.22. By comparing new observations with its forecasts, E$^2$Forecast can also detect anomalous changes without labels or retraining, raising F$_1$ from 41.58 to 48.70 on a global benchmark. This consistent superiority is validated on nine remote sensing foundation models. Beyond change detection, we believe our approach advances the field by permitting effective reuse of diverse pretrained task heads. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ucam-eo/e2forecast.

title: Accessed, never disclosed: Silent access to protected health information by medical artificial intelligence agents
comment: 33 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, 3 Extended Data tables; includes Supplementary Information (12 tables, 6 figures)
summary: Medical artificial intelligence agents should retrieve patient identifiers only when a task requires them, the data-minimization principle behind the HIPAA minimum necessary standard for protected health information (PHI). An agent can retrieve identifiers without revealing them. Such silent access remains invisible to evaluations that inspect only the output. We embedded canaries in synthetic patient records and linked each tool invocation to canary exposure in the final answers across five language models, four boundary levels, and seven attack frames for identifier-free clinical tasks. Three models invoked the PHI tools unnecessarily, whereas Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 did not. Stronger boundaries reduced this access, and the residual access under the strictest policy was confined to frames in which the user overrode the policy or asserted approval. A pre-execution gate given the task-necessity criterion nearly eliminated this access. Output-only evaluation cannot verify minimum-necessary access; boundaries, gates, and access-log audits are required together.

title: Strategist: Evolving Reasoning with Agents
summary: A model is only half of an AI agent system. The other half is the inference strategy: the reasoning procedure that turns model calls into a response. Today that second half is written by hand, and the experience of building one strategy never carries to the next. We introduce Strategist, a meta-agent that evolves inference strategies across tasks. Each strategy is written as a blueprint,executable code that other strategies can reuse, and together the blueprints form a library. Given a task and a small development set, Strategist retrieves related blueprints, writes candidate strategies, tests them on real samples, and revises them from the results. Every candidate then enters the library, so later tasks build on earlier discoveries. On 30 benchmarks, Strategist beats the strongest baseline on 24 and matches its average accuracy (74.7% vs.74.0%) at 39% lower inference cost. Its strategies also transfer to unseen tasks and other models without further search. The part of an AI system that is not improved on its own now does.

title: SVD-Prune: Spectral Vision Token Pruning under Extreme Compression
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027. Code available at https://github.com/anoncvlab/svdPrune
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models process hundreds of visual tokens, making visual representations a major computational bottleneck. We argue that visual token pruning should be formulated not as identifying individually important tokens, but as preserving the dominant low-rank spectral structure of the visual representation. Based on this formulation, we introduce SVD-Prune, a training-free framework that leverages Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and statistical leverage scores for globally informed token selection. SVD-Prune is architecture-agnostic and can be applied at different stages of the multimodal pipeline, including encoder-side, decoder-side, and hybrid configurations Extensive experiments across VLM and VLA benchmarks demonstrate strong robustness under extreme compression. SVD-Prune reduces the visual token. SVD-Prune cuts the visual token budget by up to 99.3%, while, at a 16-token budget, encoder-side pruning lowers inference FLOPs by 82.4% and achieves a 4.18x end-to-end speedup, including pruning overhead.

title: LEANGUARD: Lean-Verified Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents
summary: Tool-using language-model agents often execute actions that their domain policies forbid. We present LeanGuard, a runtime that checks every proposed tool call against a policy written in Lean4 before the call reaches the environment. Policies combine state predicates with scoped past-time temporal operators over the execution history, evaluation is fail-closed, and the decision procedure is proved equivalent to a LeanLTL semantics. A denied call can be corrected in two ways. With feedback, the agent receives the violated rule and a hint; with proof-guided repair, Lean metaprogramming searches for a nearby call that preserves the user's intent and proves that the policy admits it, without the model. On Tau-Bench with five Qwen models (0.8B-27B), unguarded agents execute at least 33 calls that the Lean policy forbids, while LeanGuard executes none; with feedback, task success does not change significantly. On DTap, LeanGuard reduces direct prompt-injection success from 57.9% to 5.9%, and in telecom, where benign tasks need no writes, benign success is unchanged. Feedback reduces repeated blocked calls and raises task success for four of five models over a bare denial. On replayed denials, repair proves an admissible edit for 88 of 252 denials caused by argument values, in a median of 2,ms.

title: WebHarbor: Docking Real Websites for Evolving GUI Agent Environments
summary: GUI web agents require realistic and interactive environments that remain stable during both evaluation and training. Live website evaluation suffers from changing content, access restrictions, and limited coverage of authenticated workflows, while existing synthetic environments for training often lack functional depth and visual fidelity. We propose WebHarbor, a suite of 153 executable and dockerized website environments that faithfully reconstruct the visual interfaces, content, and functional workflows of real-world web services under deterministic control. We build WebHarbor through task-driven human-agent collaboration, where environments evolve as new tasks expand their functional scope, coding agents implement the required changes, and human contributors audit visual fidelity, functional correctness, and task validity. The resulting suite comprises 3,518 tasks spanning multi-step and post-authentication workflows, where existing works often fail to cover. Beyond reliable evaluation, WebHarbor provides high-fidelity synthetic web environments for cost-efficient reinforcement learning (RL). We demonstrate that a Qwen 4B-level GUI agent trained with RL in WebHarbor generalizes to unseen tasks and performs competitively with leading open-source GUI web agents across four benchmarks. The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/aiming-lab/WebHarbor.

title: Peripheral prototypical contrastive loss for supervised medical image segmentation
summary: Robust segmentation of biomedical images remains challenging primarily due to ill-defined object boundaries. Although several loss functions have recently been proposed to enhance object boundary recognition, concerns remain about the susceptibility to unstable annotations resulting from boundary ambiguities. Here, we introduce the Peripheral Prototypical Contrastive (PPC) loss, which leverages prototypical contrastive learning to improve boundary recognition and enable stable training even under noisy annotation conditions. The PPC loss utilizes prototype features obtained from local regions near object boundaries, focusing specifically on ambiguous areas that have been challenging for existing approaches. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrated that the PPC loss consistently improve segmentation performance even under conditions with noisy labels. A newly proposed strategy, which adaptively determines the local region for prototype calculation, enhanced robustness and outperformed existing methods. Our findings indicate the potential of the PPC loss in facilitating scalable and reliable medical image segmentation, including the development of foundation models with imperfect annotations.

title: When Does Adaptive Halting Win? Selection Rules Matter in Looped Language Models
summary: Looped language models can stop iterating early, and recent work shows that post-hoc readouts of the loop trajectory often rival the learned exit gate of the looped model Ouro. Such comparisons reduce each method to one operating point chosen by a selection rule. We ask whether that rule decides the outcome. On a frozen Ouro-1.4B with four loops, we compared a trained stability probe ($π_1$-x) with Ouro's native gate, adapted to a per-question stopping decision, in pre-registered studies; the confirmatory study was designed after an exploratory finding on development data and evaluated once on a sealed test set of 8,517 questions. In the pre-registered confirmatory comparison, which selected operating points with a bootstrap-screened 1 pp accuracy-loss rule, the probe saved more of the four-loop budget than the native gate (+0.053 gross macro saving over three benchmarks, 95% CI [+0.049, +0.057]), mostly from CommonsenseQA, where the probe's test upper bound on accuracy loss exceeded 1 pp. Under a point-only rule, a pre-specified secondary analysis on the same test set reversed the preference (-0.022 [-0.026, -0.018]), with operating points that exceeded the budget. In pre-specified secondary comparisons, the probe showed no demonstrated advantage over an untrained KL divergence between successive loops (+0.00125 [-0.0041, +0.0065]); we emphasise this result post hoc and claim no equivalence. The probe also broke its budget on one of two out-of-distribution benchmarks (3.26 pp loss on Social IQa). Savings are estimated from stored full-depth traces, not measured inference time, and our screen carries no formal risk-control guarantee. We conclude that halting methods should be compared as signals together with selection procedures, with strong untrained baselines and out-of-distribution checks.

title: From Natural Language to Exact Cover: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Zebra Puzzles
summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation has substantially improved the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, including code generation, data analysis, and exam-style question answering. Despite these advances, purely neural LLMs continue to struggle with elementary logical reasoning problems and lack the determinism, soundness, and reliability characteristic of symbolic reasoning systems. Conversely, classical symbolic methods such as SAT solving and exact cover guarantee correctness and completeness, but require problems to be expressed in highly specialized formal encodings, limiting their applicability to natural language inputs. In this work, we present a synergistic neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by combining neural semantic parsing with deterministic exact cover reasoning. Given a Zebra-style logic puzzle in natural language, an LLM translates entities and constraints into structured tool calls that construct an exact cover instance. A symbolic solver then computes the solution and provides feedback to iteratively refine invalid, under- or overconstrained encodings, exploiting the uniqueness property of Zebra puzzles. We conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple parameter scales, post-training paradigms, and LLM families. The results demonstrate that our hybrid approach consistently outperforms strong plain neural baselines, including CoT prompting, as well as recent neuro-symbolic methods.

title: Lie Routing Vision Language Models for View-Robust 3D Understanding
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made substantial progress in 3D scene understanding from multi-view RGB observations. Yet a fixed object and query can elicit inconsistent target-related responses across camera viewpoints, a phenomenon we characterize as viewpoint-induced semantic drift. We introduce LieVLM, a Lie routing framework for view-robust 3D understanding. Motivated by the rotational component of viewpoint change, Lie routing adapts visual representations by applying local $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ transformations to projected features within learned three-dimensional subspaces. Geometry tokens extracted by VGGT predict local rotation parameters and channel-wise routing coefficients. A closed-form Padé--Cayley map transforms projected visual features, whose identity-relative corrections are projected back and gated into the original visual and geometry features. This design retains the pretrained semantic and direct spatial context while learning view-dependent feature adjustments. Experiments on 3D captioning, grounding, detection, and spatial reasoning show consistent improvements over additive fusion across training scales and backbones. Controlled ablations examine the roles of geometric conditioning and transformation structure. Viewpoint analyses further reveal systematic variation in the predicted routing states alongside more localized target responses and stronger task performance across viewpoint changes.

title: When Rewards Depend on the Group, GRPO Plays a Tournament
summary: Rewards for diversity, coverage and distribution matching make the reward of each sampled response depend on the rest of its group, and they are now routinely optimized with GRPO and RLOO. We prove that in this setting the group-relative baseline changes the objective. The expected update equals each response's own reward gradient plus $α$ times its effect on its groupmates' rewards, with $α=-1/(K-1)$ for groups of size $K$, so GRPO trains every response to beat its groupmates in a zero-sum tournament. It cannot see a pairwise diversity bonus when K=2, sees less than half of it at any K, and often does worse than using no baseline at all. Setting $α=+1$ gives Team-GRPO, an unbiased estimator for any group-dependent reward that works with two samples per prompt and requires no extra model calls for pairwise rewards. The theory predicts training quantitatively. It locates the fixed points of a 9B policy to within 0.02 in $\ell_1$ and predicts how concentrated trained policies become with Pearson r=0.995. On GlobalOpinionQA, GRPO collapses onto the majority answer and ends further from human opinion than the untrained model, while Team-GRPO cuts the error from $0.20$ to $0.08$. On NoveltyBench, Team-GRPO avoids the diversity collapse of GRPO and significantly improves set utility.

title: Output-Aware Block Influence: Jacobian-Lens Weighting for Depth Pruning
summary: Depth pruning removes entire transformer blocks and therefore depends on a reliable criterion for identifying which blocks can be removed. Block Influence (BI) ranks blocks by how minimally they rotate the hidden state. However, local redundancy does not necessarily imply downstream irrelevance. We address this limitation using the Jacobian Lens (J-Lens) neural artifact, a map transporting perturbations at a layer to the final residual stream. At a common sparsity level, pruning scores applying J-Lens transportation to $BI$, what we call $J-BI$, were found to improve post-pruning accuracy by up to 19 points over $BI$ while reducing damage to perplexity for Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-IT, and Gemma-3-12B-IT. We also perform a single-block ablation study and use J-Lens probing to explain why the proposed scores improved performance.

title: The DynaCell Evaluation Suite for Dynamic 3D Virtual Staining of Live Cells
comment: 64 pages: 10-page main text with 4 figures and 1 table, plus references and a 49-page appendix with 15 figures and 25 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets
summary: Understanding how cells respond to perturbations over time is central to cell biology and drug discovery. Live-cell imaging captures the dynamics of perturbation-induced phenotypes in individual cells. While fluorescence imaging can visualize specific molecular phenotypes, labeling and repeated illumination often affect cell health. Virtual staining offers an alternative by predicting these fluorescence images from images acquired without fluorescent labels. Although many virtual staining models have been developed, their performance on volumetric time-lapse data remains poorly characterized. We address this gap with an evaluation suite for 3D time-lapse virtual staining of live cells. The suite combines paired 3D time-lapse images acquired with and without fluorescent labels, a set of baseline models, and three metric tiers measuring pixel-level fidelity, organelle segmentation performance, and single-cell phenotype similarity. Using this evaluation suite, we study metric and model behavior across 3 cell types, 2 microscopes, 4 organelles, and 3 perturbation states. We find that regression baselines better predict the spatial localization of target organelles, whereas the generative baseline better captures the distribution of phenotypes across cells. These differences expose trade-offs between structural and phenotypic fidelity that are obscured by single-metric evaluation and suggest how virtual staining models can be developed for diverse downstream tasks such as localization, segmentation, tracking, and phenotypic profiling. We release the curated datasets, baseline checkpoints, and evaluation code as part of DynaCell, a broader framework for image-based profiling of cell-state dynamics.

title: InteractionBench: Measuring Timing, Task Accuracy, Whisper and Volume, and Grounding in Real-Time Voice Systems
summary: Most benchmarks for real-time voice systems focus on one aspect, such as turn-taking, instruction following, paralinguistic control, or conversational memory, each with its own data and set of systems. We present InteractionBench, a benchmark and evaluation harness that measures four dimensions on the same systems from the same recorded user audio: conversational timing, spoken-task accuracy, whisper and volume, and groundedness in conversations of more than twenty turns. The benchmark contains 221 items per system in thirteen scenarios. Before any system runs, we fix the expected floor-control actions for spoken tasks by rule and take the expected answers from scripted dialogues. We score whispering from the audio signal. We evaluate GPT-Live, GPT-Realtime, Gemini Live, Moshi, PersonaPlex, Freeze-Omni, and a turn-based cascade in 1,519 graded runs. Among the six full-duplex systems, timing and spoken-task accuracy are rank-correlated ($ρ= 0.83$), while the cascade has the highest spoken-task score (38/50) and the second-lowest timing score. No system corrects a user's grammar within the required window. Only Gemini Live whispers on most requests (8/10). Hosted systems pass 67-88% of groundedness probes, compared with 14-35% for open full-duplex models. Timing is measured where the client hears each system, so the timing of hosted systems includes network delay: for GPT-Live, whose server reports its own clock, removing a delay of about 1.5 s lowers its timing score from 86% to 56%. We also document where the protocol differs across systems, including the text instructions.

title: Beyond the Last Layer: Global Inter-Layer Aggregation for AI-Generated Image Detection
summary: The rapid development of generative models has made AI-generated images increasingly close to real images. It has also brought several challenges to detectors, including rapid generator updates, large changes in data distribution, and limited cross-dataset generalization. Many existing methods based on pretrained vision encoders primarily use the global representation from the last layer, potentially leaving useful information from intermediate layers underexplored. To address this issue, we propose Global Inter-Layer Aggregation (GILA). GILA extracts global representations from different depths of a frozen encoder, models interactions among layer representations through inter-layer self-attention, and adaptively aggregates the resulting contextualized representations. The method is not tied to a single pretraining objective and does not require fine-tuning the pretrained encoder. We evaluated GILA on three vision backbones with different pretraining objectives, ten seen generators, and three external datasets. The experimental results show that GILA makes better use of multi-layer information in pretrained encoders and improves detection performance and cross-dataset generalization.

title: Findings-aware Language-Image Pretraining for CT Volume Interpretation
summary: Computed tomography (CT) provides diverse patient information and various clinical tasks, for which numerous deep learning models have been investigated. Recent years have seen the development of vision-language foundation models that can comprehensively extract clinical features, driven by representation learning that combines CT volumes with radiology reports. Existing approaches typically adopt Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP)-based representation learning, where pairs from different cases are, in principle, treated as negative pairs such that the volume and report embeddings are pushed apart. In the biomedical imaging, however, treating different cases as negative pairs is not always appropriate, particularly when clinical similarity exists. In this study, we propose a supervised representation learning framework grounded in clinical knowledge from language foundation models, rather than the weak supervision used in CLIP. Specifically, we utilized a large language model to extract abnormal finding phrases from reports. We then explicitly constructed the target features that the image encoder should output, as the semantic representation of the extracted findings using a biomedical text embedding model. Our Findings-aware Language-Image Pre-training (FiLIP) outperformed weakly supervised approaches in multi-label zero-shot finding classification in both in-domain and external-domain evaluations, and also proved effective when fine-tuned for the downstream task of radiology report generation.

title: PixelBench: Can LLMs Understand and Generate Images Pixel by Pixel?
comment: Technical report, 38 pages, 7 figures. Project page: https://haoquanzhang.github.io/pixel-bench
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate visual assets through text-based formats such as SVG and CAD, but these symbolic representations describe images using high-level primitives rather than explicit raster values. We ask whether LLMs can instead generate pixel images directly through their existing vocabulary, without a learned image tokenizer or decoder. We introduce PixelBench, a benchmark for text-to-pixel (T2P) and image-to-pixel (I2P) generation across multiple resolutions, together with a complementary pixel-understanding evaluation. Models generate an RGB color palette followed by a grid of indices specifying the palette color of each output pixel. In T2P, the strongest models produce recognizable images directly from text. In I2P, the strongest models outperform palette-matched downsampling and specialized pixelization algorithms at low resolutions. Pixel-understanding performance correlates strongly with generation performance. A resolution-scaling study shows that pixel-generation performance often improves initially before declining at high resolutions. Finally, we introduce Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT), which augments visual instruction tuning with caption-palette-grid trajectories. We post-train Molmo2-4B from its pretraining checkpoint by mixing general instruction data with our curated PRT data, improving performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks, indicating that explicit pixel reconstruction can provide useful auxiliary supervision.

title: Intervenable Concept Dynamics for Video Activity Forecasting
summary: Concept bottleneck models route predictions through human-understandable concepts, making their intermediate states inspectable and editable. Extending this model family to forecasting requires modeling how concept activations evolve over time as objects, actions, and their interactions change, yet existing CBMs ground concepts only in observed inputs and do not forecast their future evolution. We study this problem using videos of ongoing activities and forecast future activities through a named-concept state. We propose TRACE-CBM (Temporal Relational Activity Concept Evolution), which first refines observed concept activations with sparse spatio-temporal graphs. It then recursively predicts future concept states, conditioning each transition on the prior activity distribution, and decodes both observed and predicted states with a shared activity classifier. At inference time, the model supports editing concept values, activity activations, and learned edges without parameter updates, exposing the relational spatio-temporal dependencies used for forecasting. Across multiple datasets, TRACE improves observed-activity Top-1 accuracy over concept-based methods by 1.2-8.5 percentage points and attains H3 forecast Top-1 accuracy within 1.9-2.2 points of matched black-box forecasters. Intervention experiments show concept-node edits correct 25.6-34.4% of initially incorrect H3 forecasts without flipping initially correct ones, and concept steering achieves the requested target activity in up to 90.0% of cases.

title: AgiWorld: An Agentic Video World Model for Building Persistent Worlds
summary: Recent interactive video world models generate visually compelling videos from a single image, following user-provided camera motion and text prompts. However, such low-level control demands substantial user effort to realize a high-level intent, and the generated world struggles to remain persistent as the exploration proceeds. In this work, we present AgiWorld, an agentic video world model that explores and builds a persistent world from a single image and a free-form instruction. For high-level planning, our agent AgiWorld-Agent designs the world and the journey through it in a world state and directs the exploration. For low-level realization, our video world model AgiWorld-WM generates the video chunk by chunk and stores it with its geometry in a spatial memory, from which the agent updates its world state. This closed loop keeps the world faithful to the user's intent and keeps the agent's world state consistent with the generated content throughout the exploration. We co-design the two levels around the shared spatial memory and an interface of metric camera trajectories and structured prompts. In AgiWorld-WM, to handle occlusion and accumulated geometric errors in the spatial memory over long rollouts, we propose occlusion-aware history selection, which retrieves past views by surface visibility, and reliability-based memory maintenance, which prefers reliable geometry and earlier observations. AgiWorld-WM achieves state-of-the-art overall performance on world revisiting and exploration benchmarks, and qualitative results and ablations show that AgiWorld builds persistent worlds from free-form instructions over minute-long journeys. Persistence thus arises not from the video model alone but from its closed loop with the agent.

title: SMILE: A Structured Multi-Agent Clinical Reasoning for Liver Ultrasound Understanding
comment: Accepted at Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) 2027
summary: Automated liver ultrasound report generation improves the diagnosis of liver diseases by producing clinically structured descriptions of anatomical and disease-related findings. However, current generative vision-language models (VLMs) often rely on a single reasoning pathway that maps ultrasound appearance directly to textual descriptions. In addition to the inherent vision-language modality gap, this design is limited for liver ultrasound because disease interpretation is constrained by subtle visual evidence, heterogeneous disease patterns, and limited paired supervision. To address these limitations, we propose SMILE, a Structured Multi-agent clInicaL rEasoning framework that uses multiple complementary specialist agents to interpret ultrasound images and consolidates their outputs through a judge-guided consensus mechanism. Our approach employs three specialized agents: an image interpretation agent for morphological descriptions, a clinical-stage reasoning agent, and a visual question answering (VQA) agent for targeted queries. These agent responses are then aggregated and scrutinized by a judge VLM using a consensus filtering prompt to produce a unified, clinically coherent output. Across a public liver ultrasound dataset and an internal clinical dataset, SMILE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art VLMs, achieving up to 19.0\% improvement in ROUGE-1 and 18.8\% improvement in clinical F1-score, while reaching VQA F1-scores of 0.82 and 0.65 on public and internal datasets, respectively. These results demonstrate the potential of SMILE for data-scarce and limited-supervision clinical settings. Our models, datasets, and code are available \href{https://github.com/CMME-Lab/SMILE}{here}.

title: SFA: A Statistical Physics-Inspired Diffusion Transformer for Efficient and High-Quality Image Generation
summary: Diffusion transformers have achieved remarkable success in image generation, but accelerating attention while preserving generation quality remains a major challenge at high resolutions. Inspired by statistical physics and the widespread occurrence of scale-free laws in nature, we introduce Scale-Free Attention (SFA), which preserves fine local interactions while summarizing distant regions at progressively coarser scales. For $N$ tokens, mean pooling, token-count correction, and a shared softmax over a scale-free spatial hierarchy give SFA $O(N\log N)$ complexity in both forward and backward passes. Our Triton implementation achieves $357.3\times$ forward and $265.6\times$ backward attention speedups over FlashAttention at 262,144 tokens. After 40 epochs of PixelFlow training from scratch on ImageNet at $256\times256$ resolution, SFA achieves the best generation quality among five attention mechanisms, including full attention. Fréchet inception distance evaluated on 50,000 generated samples (FID-50k) improves from 13.25 for full attention to 12.51, and the advantage over full attention persists through 80 epochs. SFA also achieves the best generation quality among the compared efficient-attention methods on Flickr-Faces-HQ (FFHQ). Beyond training from scratch, Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium with attention replaced by SFA retains the generation quality of its full-attention counterpart under matched fine-tuning budgets. We obtain similar results when fine-tuning pretrained PixelFlow on ImageNet. SFA establishes scale-free structure as an effective design principle for efficient, high-quality diffusion transformers.

title: Exploiting Textual Semantics for Robust Cross-View Object Correspondence
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 12 figures, 12 tables. Code: https://github.com/VAIL-Fan/TeSCo
summary: Cross-view object correspondence (CVOC) aims to establish associations of the same target between query and search videos captured from different viewpoints. Existing methods often rely on visual cues for CVOC. Despite recent progress, these methods struggle in complicated scenarios with substantial viewpoint changes and appearance variations, due to lacking sufficient target information. Addressing this, we introduce TeSCo, a framework that exploits rich Textual Semantics of an object, in addition to its visual cues, for cross-view object Correspondence. Our key insight is, textual description of a target, by capturing diverse attributes such as category, texture, and color, provides viewpoint- and appearance-invariant semantics, which are complementary to visual cues and can hence enhance correspondence robustness in complicated scenes. Inspired by this, TeSCo first generates a textual expression of the target from the given query view using a vision-language model, and then extracts textual feature to enhance visual features for localization in the search view. To realize this, we introduce a text-conditioned cross-modal fusion (TCF) module that incorporates the textual feature into visual features with text-guided modulation, producing more robust multimodal target representation for object correspondence. Since not all textual cues are equally compatible with the target in current search-view frame, we propose an iterative textual feature refinement (ITFR) module that progressively adjusts textual feature using search-view information before the TCF module, enabling search-view-aware textual semantics to be fused into visual features and leading to better performance. In extensive experiments on Ego-Exo4D and HANDAL-X, TeSCo demonstrates state-of-the-art results and largely outperforms other models, validating its efficacy. Our code is released at https://github.com/VAIL-Fan/TeSCo.

title: Variable names provide priors: semantic grounding enables data-efficient numerical prediction by large language models
comment: Main text: 30 pages, 6 figures. Supplementary information: 53 pages, 11 figures
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across diverse tasks, from question answering to code generation. Recent studies have found that LLMs can perform numerical prediction on tabular datasets via in-context learning. However, it remains unclear under what conditions and how LLMs use variable names and in-context examples for numerical prediction. Here we show that semantic grounding, the match between variable names and the values they describe, allows five LLMs without task-specific training to match or outperform seven supervised machine learning (ML) models across 20 datasets from nine scientific domains, particularly when examples are scarce. Reasoning traces indicate that variable names allow LLMs to draw on domain-specific knowledge acquired during pretraining. Using controlled tasks based on physical formulas, we further show that LLMs integrate domain-specific knowledge with in-context examples in a way consistent with Bayesian updating. Specifically, when the relationship between the inputs and the target cannot be inferred from the examples alone, LLMs rely on domain-specific knowledge as the prior. Conversely, as contradicting examples accumulate, LLM predictions shift progressively towards these examples, which act as the likelihood. Our work reveals how LLMs use domain-specific knowledge in numerical prediction and positions them as data-efficient predictors for data-scarce scientific domains.

title: A Trustworthy Clinical Decision Support Framework for Brain Tumor MRI Classification: Integrating Attention-Guided Learning, Explainable AI, and Out-of-Distribution Validation
comment: Accepted for presentation at the IC3AI-2026 IEEE conference in Dec 2026. It has been accepted/selected but is not yet published. 6 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables
summary: Deep learning models for brain tumor diagnosis need to do more than achieve high classification accuracy. For practical use, they should also provide understandable predictions, recognize unsuitable inputs, and work within a usable clinical system. This paper presents a framework for classifying brain MRI into four categories: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor. The model uses InceptionResNetV2 with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM), while Grad-CAM provides visual explanations of its predictions. A two-stage out-of-distribution (OOD) mechanism screens unsuitable inputs using an initial grayscale check followed by Mahalanobis distance, softmax confidence, and predictive entropy. These components are brought together in NeuroScan AI, a real-time web application. Evaluated on a Mendeley brain tumor MRI dataset of 12,064 images, the framework achieved 98.70% validation accuracy, 96.73% test accuracy, and a macro-average AUC of 0.9965. The OOD pipeline achieved 99% detection accuracy on a preliminary 100-image benchmark. Grad-CAM visualizations showed qualitative correspondence with clinically established tumor locations across all four classes. Overall, the work brings classification, explainability, input validation, and deployment into one framework, while recognizing that broader clinical and OOD validation is still required.

title: GEAR: Generative Editing for Scene-Conditioned Outfit Retrieval for VR Travel
summary: In virtual environments, choosing appropriate outfits requires contextual harmony with surrounding scenes, yet bridging the visual gap between 3D ambient views and catalog garment assets remains challenging. This paper investigates scene-conditioned outfit retrieval for interactive 3D environments, where a user's egocentric view serves as the retrieval signal. We present GEAR (Generative Editing for Asset Retrieval), a framework that bridges the cross-domain gap by synthesizing intermediate visual queries rather than predicting direct compatibility. GEAR uses a vision-language model to describe suitable clothing from a captured scene, employs an instruction-guided diffusion model to render the concept onto a standardized reference character, and utilizes the cropped clothing region to retrieve existing 2D outfit assets via embedding similarity. An interactive Unity prototype demonstrates real-time scene capture, asset retrieval, and in-engine 3D avatar fitting. We benchmark GEAR against direct visual similarity, aesthetic scoring, and VLM-based reranking on a controlled dataset using automated Swiss-system pairwise judgments, where GEAR achieves competitive top-ranked performance (mean Elo@5 of 1012.75 and top-10 overlap of 0.180) alongside 0.539 pairwise agreement. Furthermore, a user study across 20 virtual travel scenes demonstrates that GEAR achieves the highest overall participant preference in both visual appeal (34.5%) and contextual suitability (34.5%).

title: Constructing an Artworld Influencers Network by Mining Social Media
comment: Author's accepted manuscript. Published in Leonardo 55(1), 24-29 (2022), MIT Press. (c) 2022 ISAST. Supplemental material and tweet IDs: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23586408
summary: The author shows a methodology for constructing a network map of the artworld. The tweets posted by a manually comprised set of exemplar artworld actors and Natural Language Processing (NLP) methods are used to identify significant artworld actors, including those that do not own a Twitter account. Identified artworld actors form communities detected with the Louvain method, and their authority is evaluated with the HITS centrality method. The resulting artworld network exhibits the ability, starting with a small set of exemplar actors, to identify new artworld actors and provides a wealth of data that would be very hard to collect otherwise.

title: From Single-Shot QA to Continuous Perception: Revisiting the Energy Composition and Optimization Boundary of Edge VLMs
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at IEEE International Conference on Data Mining 2026 Teen Research Track
summary: Visual-prefill energy conclusions for edge vision-language models (VLMs) are commonly drawn under single-shot workloads; we revisit them under continuous perception. Profiling nine VLMs across three architecture families on Jetson AGX Thor and Orin (4,508 records, calibrated with a pure-text task), we find two mutually independent energy laws: the per-output-token decode cost grows monotonically with model scale, whereas the visual-prefill (image-encoding) cost is dominated by visual-encoder architectural efficiency, not scale. Under continuous perception ($N{=}10$) with sparse output, visual-prefill energy reaches 92--97\% of total. We derive optimization strategies---visual frame reuse, adaptive output truncation, task-aware routing, and encoder throughput optimization---for edge VLM deployment.

title: IMUdrape: Generating Garment-Mounted Virtual IMU Data from Text through Physics-Based Cloth Simulation
comment: 34 pages, 7 figures, 15 tables. Under review. Project page: https://zikangleng.github.io/imudrape/
summary: Inertial sensors are moving into clothing, from sensorized sportswear to garments instrumented with hundreds of IMUs. Sewn into clothing, a sensor no longer moves rigidly with the body: loose fabric slides, twists and swings, so a garment-mounted sensor records the motion of the fabric as well as that of the body, and this extra motion differs from one garment to the next. Models for such sensors need training data recorded with the deployed garment, yet labeled data are scarce. Virtual IMU data generated from videos or text have eased this scarcity for body-attached sensors, but existing generators attach their virtual sensors rigidly to the body. We present IMUdrape, which generates garment-mounted virtual IMU data from text through physics-based cloth simulation. IMUdrape synthesizes motion from activity descriptions, reconstructs the target garment as a sewing pattern from photographs, places virtual IMUs at the deployment's real sensor positions, and simulates the garment with an intersection-free contact solver, so that every simulation yields paired garment and body signals. On four real datasets with clothing-mounted sensors, IMUdrape improves on existing virtual-data approaches for both activity recognition and full-body pose estimation. With one real subject, its data improve recognition macro-F1 by 7% to 46% over real data alone and by 2% to 11% over body-mounted virtual data from the same motion. When the garment is simulated on recorded motion, the pose error without any real training data falls by 30% to 33% relative to generated motion, and garment data remain 12% more accurate than body data. IMUdrape thus reduces the amount of real data that garment-mounted sensing requires.

title: Train the Sampler You Run: Few-Step Masked Diffusion Language Models via Mixture-Likelihood Fine-Tuning
summary: When a masked diffusion language model is sampled in a few parallel steps in a random order, the model actually run is a mixture over reveal plans, while cross-entropy training fits token conditionals rather than this mixture. We introduce mixture-likelihood fine-tuning (Mix-FT), which fine-tunes a pretrained model on an importance-weighted bound of its own sampler's likelihood, with no teacher and no change to the architecture or the sampler. On LLaDA-8B, a LoRA fine-tune for 0.002% of the pretraining compute writes better OpenWebText continuations than continued cross-entropy and Alpha diffusion given the same compute, at every tested step count. With half the model evaluations, 16 rather than 32 steps per block, its continuations score better than the original model's in every seed under three judges, with confidence-based decoding as well as random order, and under confidence-based decoding two blinded LLM raters from different model families prefer them in 69 and 71% of pairs. On a public 110M-parameter block diffusion model, Mix-FT takes under four T4-hours and beats continued cross-entropy, Alpha diffusion and SDTT distillation at 4, 8 and 16 steps per block, under two judges in every seed. Exact likelihoods on text8, with a control that weights every plan equally, attribute about three quarters of the likelihood gain over continued cross-entropy to weighting each plan by how well it explains the sequence.

title: Beyond Black Boxes: An Ontology Based Vision Framework for Transparent Fruit Disease Detection
summary: Efficiency and reliability in the timely identification of phytopathogens would help minimize crop loss in agricultural sectors but existing deep learning based methods, although accurate, would require a large annotated dataset and are black-boxed in their operation, thus, restricting flexibility and transparency. The current paper presents a hybrid detection framework that is able to overcome these drawbacks through the unified real-time vision with a semantic knowledge base. Web Ontology Language (OWL) was used to develop a comprehensive ontology of the disease of fruits that formally codifies phytopathological knowledge, such as symptom phenotype, spectral phenotype (HSV), and morphological phenotype. Such knowledge-guided configuration guides the image processing pipeline, making it possible to diagnose using this knowledge under expert specified rules without a large training dataset. The ontology underwent a computationally verified test of its structural soundness and commonsensical practical usefulness and scored an overall of 7.4/10. On the public set of MangoFruitDDS, the diagnostic performance was an F1 Score of 85.00%, precision of 85.00%, and a recall of 85.23%. These findings are very competitive and similar to other known deep learning models like the VGG16 that prove that the knowledge-driven approach provides an accurate, transparent, and scalable solution on automated fruit disease diagnosis.

title: TERA: Task-Evidence Restoration for Underwater Object Detection under Bandwidth-Constrained Transmission
summary: Underwater object detectors are typically evaluated on pre-transmission images, overlooking additional degradation from bandwidth-constrained downscaling and compression. We introduce AquaTX, a controlled benchmark built from real underwater detection datasets with seen and held-out codecs. We also propose TERA, a metadata-blind receiver-side framework combining task-guided pixel restoration and dual-state feature correction while keeping the detector frozen. Under seen compound degradation, TERA improves mean average precision (mAP50:95, averaged over IoU thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95) from 37.7 to 50.0 on DUO-TX and from 31.5 to 41.3 on RUOD-TX relative to the frozen detector without restoration. TERA also preserves clean-input performance and remains competitive with detector fine-tuning under the held-out AVIF codec. These findings support transmission-aware evaluation and task-guided restoration for underwater object detection. Code is available at https://github.com/hijinkim/TERA.

title: Replay for LLM Continual Learning with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) distills domain experts into one student but needs every expert at once. When domains arrive one at a time and earlier experts are gone, the previous-stage student can teach replayed prompts of earlier domains inside every stage. Some pipelines instead store every stage snapshot for a final multi-teacher recovery stage. On five domains with a 1.5B student and five public experts, this paper compares both with joint MOPD. It varies the replay budget and the replay signal. The signal is token-level distillation alone or with alignment of hidden states, attention and value relations. Sequential distillation without replay or recovery is 6.2 points below 208-step joint MOPD on a 14-benchmark average and 3.5 points below on the 11 benchmarks outside safety. Without snapshots, replay toward the previous student closes 3.8 of the 6.2 points when the earlier domains share the replay budget of a stage. With a fixed share of seven replay steps per earlier domain and stage, it closes 5.8 over two training runs. This is level with the 5.9 of recovery from all snapshots, both at its default length and when given as many training steps as the fixed share. Alignment terms on replay steps change the average by about one point or less. If refusal and compliance count equally in safety, shared-budget replay ranks first among the trained configurations, and the fixed share stays at or above recovery. Against the shared budget, the fixed share lowers the score on the newest domain. Recovery lowers this score as well, in five of six cases. The replay steps of the fixed share grow quadratically with the number of stages.

title: Real-Time Obstacle Detection and Distance Estimation on Smartphones for Visually Impaired and Distracted Pedestrians
summary: According to the World Health Organization, at least 2.2 billion people worldwide live with visual impairment, including tens of millions with severe vision loss. Traditional aids such as white canes or guide dogs remain costly, limited in capability, and inaccessible to many. At the same time, smartphone distraction in public spaces has been linked to elevated risks of collisions with vehicles, trips, and falls. These dual challenges motivate lightweight, smartphone-based solutions that combine accessibility with low latency. We present a Kotlin-based Android application that uses a YOLOv8 detector, retrained to recognize eighteen common urban obstacle classes, to deliver real-time obstacle alerts for both user groups. The detector was optimized with pruning, quantization, and early-exit branches, and deployed through the Android Neural Networks API (NNAPI), which can dispatch inference to GPU, NPU, or DSP accelerators when available. On a mid-range smartphone, these optimizations reduced average inference latency from about 3.2 s for the off-the-shelf YOLOv8n to 0.39-0.48 s; the recommended configuration (INT8 quantization with early exit) runs in 0.42-0.48 s while retaining a recall of 0.81. The application combines the optimized detector with ARCore-based or monocular focal-length distance estimation, so it works with a single smartphone camera and requires no LiDAR, depth camera, or other specialized sensor. Multimodal feedback, including Text-to-Speech guidance for visually impaired users and vibration alerts for distracted pedestrians, supports use across different contexts.

title: Blueprint2CAD: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Engineering Drawing-to-CAD Render Correspondence
summary: Engineering drawings specify mechanical parts through orthographic projections. Recognizing which part a drawing depicts underlies part search, design reuse, and digitization, yet no public benchmark measures whether vision models can do it. We introduce Blueprint2CAD, a benchmark for drawing-to-render correspondence: given an orthographic line drawing and a shaded render, usually from another viewpoint, decide whether they show the same part. Its data layer, BlueCAD-30K, applies an open drafting pipeline to 29,925 Zero-to-CAD models, adding view-aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings from six viewpoints, and surface-type metadata. Frozen encoders retrieve the matching part from a 10,000-model gallery with up to 65% Recall@1 when viewpoints are known but 43% when they are not, and the four encoders we test lie within six points of each other: viewpoint, not backbone, is the bottleneck. Six zero-shot vision-language models reach only 0.52-0.67 verification accuracy, with model-specific Yes/No biases that chain-of-thought shifts but does not remove; a quick LoRA fine-tuning on in-domain pairs improves verification accuracy by a few points but sharpens these biases and leaves the viewpoint failure intact.

title: Stop Handcrafting Your Engine! GenDB-V: Towards AI-Generated and Formally Verified Database Systems
summary: For over 50 years, the database community has developed a wide range of successful engines to answer two fundamental questions: how can database systems run faster, and how can we ensure their correctness? Experience with these engines shows that performance depends on hardware and workloads. As both change over time, we repeatedly redesign and rebuild database systems, a time-consuming and expensive process. Correctness remains another long-standing challenge: recent studies continue to uncover wrong-answer bugs even in mature database engines, despite years of development and testing. To address these, we present GenDB-V, a system that enables AI agents to synthesize database engines specialized to hardware and workloads for performance, and formally verified for correctness. GenDB-V supports specialized implementations of SQL templates and general-purpose engines that accept any query within a supported SQL subset. First, we develop SQLSpec to formalize SQL semantics and deterministically construct fixed, implementation-agnostic synthesis targets. Second, we enable joint synthesis of fast code and formal proofs through storage--execution co-optimization, performance-first exploration, and three-layer modular proofs that bridge low-level execution to SQLSpec semantics. Third, we verify the synthesized code and proofs against the fixed synthesis targets in an isolated pipeline, proving SQL correctness and program safety. We evaluate GenDB-V on TPC-H and SEC-EDGAR. For verified template implementations, GenDB-V achieves geometric-mean speedups of 22.0-61.3x over DuckDB and Umbra. For a verified general-purpose engine, GenDB-V also achieves speedups of 1.27-3.4x on TPC-H. GenDB-V also achieves better performance than a testing-based LLM synthesis method, while our audit and tests expose incorrect answers in that method's implementations for 16 of 28 templates.

title: Think Before You Locate: Clinical Chain-of-Though Supervision for Sequential Medical Image Grounding
summary: Clinicians rarely localize a finding from one image alone. They compare current and prior scans, follow structures across slices, and match regions across views or modalities. Yet vision-language models for sequential medical grounding usually learn only from bounding boxes. Boxes show where the target is, but they do not explain why that region in that image answers the question. We study whether explicit, image-grounded reasoning can improve localization, and which tasks benefit from it. We introduce method, whose core is MedChain, a corpus of 182,573 filtered rationales spanning eight sequential grounding tasks and ten imaging modalities. A medical VLM (FlemingVL-38B) first drafts a caption-like rationale, and a multimodal refiner (Qwen3.5-397B-A17B) then re-examines the images, question and annotated box to write a box-conditioned explanation with explicit cross-image reasoning. We fine-tune Qwen3.5 on these rationales with deliberative chain-of-thought supervision (dCoT-SFT). Across 4B, 9B, and 27B models, dCoT-SFT sets a new state of the art on MedSG-Bench. The 27B model reaches 77.24 mIoU and 85.20 Acc@0.5, improving over the strongest prior model by 4.69 and 5.49 points. In a paired comparison using fixed 4B checkpoints, dCoT-SFT improves over answer-only SFT by 3.56 mIoU (95% CI 3.13--4.00). The gains mainly come from change detection and object tracking, while performance drops on three appearance-matching tasks. Replacing a model's own rationale with a rationale from another task reduces mIoU by 12.2 points, showing that localization depends strongly on the reasoning context. Finally, adding GRPO with an IoU reward after dCoT-SFT gives only small and task-dependent gains, which we analyze through controlled multi-seed development experiments.

title: Evaluating Synthetic Skin Lesion Images for Classifier Training: A Safety-Aware Algorithm
comment: 57 pages, 12 figures. Code to reproduce all experiments, along with links to the full Zenodo dataset and the synth-curator package, can be found at https://github.com/Amixdu/synth-curator-paper
summary: Skin cancer classifiers need large sets of annotated images, which are scarce, especially for rare lesion types. AI-generated images can fill the gap, but a generator produces images of widely varying quality, so selecting which images to retain is important. That choice usually rests on a single quality score, most often the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), which has not been tested against what a classifier needs and cannot tell whether the generator memorizes its training photographs. We test that practice with a tournament of 16 quality metrics. Each metric alone selects a training subset from a pool of 275,472 images generated by a diffusion model (EDM2), and a classifier trained on each subset scores the metric per class. The tournament shows that no single metric serves every class: FID computed on Inception features gives the best classifier for one lesion type and no measurable advantage over random sampling for another, and the generation setting it prefers is also the one closest to the training images. We turn these per-class measurements into a safety-aware evaluation algorithm that weights each metric by its measured value in each class and removes images too close to a real training image. On the held-out ISIC-2018 test set, the algorithm improves Macro-$F_2$, a recall-weighted measure of classification performance, over the FID baseline for a Swin-B classifier by +0.0136 to +0.0164 across four safety thresholds (Bonferroni-corrected $p < 0.02$) and over random sampling by about +0.03, though not for ResNet-50. Tightening the threshold improves a memorization-safety score with no measurable change in utility, but every curated set remains less safe than random sampling. The results show a modest but statistically significant gain on the primary classifier, and offer a practical, safety-aware procedure for evaluating and using synthetic data.

title: SelfImprove-Bench: Evaluating Generalization in Self-Improving Agents
summary: Recursively self-improving (RSI) systems are increasingly viewed as a promising means of accelerating progress toward artificial general intelligence. They aim to autonomously improve their capabilities by refining their working pipelines and recursively improving the strategies that guide subsequent refinements, with gains generalizing to unseen scenarios.However, existing evaluations lack reliable metrics to distinguish capability gains from scenario fitting, sustainable and extensible protocols for unseen tasks and difficulties, and fine-grained attribution of improvement to evolution traces. To this end, we propose SelfImprove-Bench,an RSI evaluation framework that organizes tasks into three primary capabilities (i.e., Exploring, Planning, Reasoning) as scenarios for guiding model evolution. We instantiated the tasks on games for controllability and reproducibility, and pairs them with scalable generation and orchestration driven by task templates and difficulty coefficients. Beyond task-level scores, SelfImprove-Bench organizes evaluation into generalization ladder levels G0 to G4 that measure how far gains transfer from training conditions. Experiments reveal that the evolutionary gains of existing RSI methods are inconsistent across generalization levels.

title: Out-of-distribution AI-generated image detection with zero-phase deconvolution for residual whitening
summary: Current AI-generated image detection methods struggle in out-of-distribution testing conditions because detectors are usually not robust when evaluated on generators not included in the training set. This work explores a way to mitigate the forensic bias between sources of images -whether real or generated -by removing generator-specific fingerprints. This new training process can be approximated by pre-processing involving a deconvolution operation designed to remove correlated noise patterns inducing loss of generalization. Indeed, we show that whitening the spatial distribution of the image noise residuals can significantly improve the performance of detectors on images coming from generators unseen during training. In particular, an end-to-end CNN model trained on whitened image residuals improves detection by 12.6% on average compared to a training involving original images.

title: Gnomon4D: Learning Where and When to Focus for Geometric Motion-Grounded World-Action Modeling
summary: World-action models (WAMs) use video-generation priors to jointly predict future observations and robot actions. Yet RGB futures entangle physical state changes with appearance, while frame-wise depth and point maps lack temporal correspondence. Existing 4D approaches either keep motion implicit in visual features or translate predicted traces into actions through a separate interface. We present Gnomon4D, a WAM that jointly generates future video, robot actions, and GeoDelta, a video-aligned 4D geometric motion field encoding the cross-frame image-plane displacement and depth change of embodiment and object points. By placing embodiment motion and object responses in a shared space, GeoDelta exposes their motion relations to the action expert at inference. Interaction-Salient Attention (InSAttn) uses these relations to focus spatial readout on task-relevant interaction regions, while Transition-Anchored Aggregation (TransAgg) aggregates evidence around changes in their relative motion, such as grasp and release. GeoDelta describes surface motion independently of embodiment-specific controls, providing a shared human--robot quasi-action for action-free pretraining on EgoManip-5000H followed by robot mid-training on Robot-30H. Gnomon4D leads on RoboTwin~2.0, VLABench, and RoboDojo, and outperforms the strongest real-robot baseline by 7.0 and 16.0 percentage points under in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, respectively.

title: Creating Hybrid Interactive Narrative Systems with LLM: From Formal Description to Evaluation
summary: Interactive narratives let users shape a story while an Experience Manager (EM) keeps it coherent, balancing player freedom against authorial control. Large Language Models now enable a new generation of hybrid EMs, which combine run-time generation from free-text input with symbolic narrative control. However, their heterogeneity makes them hard to compare: A manager's behaviour is generally tied to the unique and specific scenario in which it operates, and much of its decision-making takes place outside of any explicit and verifiable structure. We address this with an LLM-based narrative platform whose managers are interchangeable modules operating over a shared symbolic world model of facts, operations, and goals. Because every applied operation carries explicit preconditions and effects, each session can be analysed as a plan through a common state-transition representation and evaluated, independently of how the manager works internally, with shared indicators of four properties: player agency, EM controllability, author intent, and robustness. We implement three contrasting managers, based respectively on open generation, Monte Carlo repair, and autonomous characters, and compare them through functional analysis on an interactive Little Red Riding Hood scenario. The results show that no manager dominates on every property, giving authors and EM designers a concrete basis to select a manager according to their priorities.

title: ReactionBench: A Human-Anchored Benchmark for Modeling Reactions to Video
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Evaluation of Interactive Agents (IAEval). 49 pages (10 main text), 9 figures, 46 tables. Project page: https://yibozh.github.io/ReactionBench-page/
summary: Understanding what happens in a video is not sufficient for socially responsive multimodal systems: such systems also aim to relate what a person observes to how that person responds. Existing video benchmarks largely evaluate events, temporal reasoning, or people depicted in the video, while affective and viewer-response datasets often focus on emotion labels, aggregate responses, or prediction from the stimulus alone. This leaves an underexplored question: can current multimodal models ground an observed viewer reaction in the stimulus context associated with it? We introduce ReactionBench, a human-anchored benchmark for reaction-specific video understanding. Built from a candidate pool of 31,834 synchronized stimulus-reaction clips spanning 433 hours and eight domains, ReactionBench evaluates three complementary abilities: ranking the intensity of a viewer's reactions within a video, matching a reaction to its temporally aligned stimulus, and explaining the concrete stimulus cues linked to that reaction. Human annotation provides 14,894 ratings over 3,257 moments, and the frozen evaluation comprises 250 intensity profiles, 112 matching items, and 200 rationale items with 447 blind-written human references. Across seven multimodal models, reaction-specific grounding remains challenging: the best model reaches 50.9% accuracy on four-way stimulus-reaction matching, while GPT-5 shows no detectable loss under reaction substitution. Performance is also sensitive to evaluation protocol. Project page: https://yibozh.github.io/ReactionBench-page/

title: Fast-Slow Evolutionary Occupancy Prediction via Controlled Dynamics
summary: 3D semantic occupancy prediction provides dense geometric and semantic scene representations for autonomous driving, where both high accuracy and low response latency are crucial for safe downstream forecasting and planning. Existing methods usually exhibit different accuracy-latency characteristics. Performance-oriented models provide stronger geometric and semantic predictions, while deployment-friendly models provide faster responses. This motivates EvoOcc, a fast-slow evolutionary occupancy prediction framework that jointly exploits their complementary strengths to improve the accuracy-latency balance without changing the upstream architectures. EvoOcc models evolutionary occupancy prediction as a continuous time controlled dynamical system, enabling flexible adaptation to variable slow system delays and irregular fast system arrivals. The framework further decomposes the evolution process into dual state evolution where ego state evolution compensates for the deterministic coordinate shifts and scene state evolution models the genuine geometric and semantic scene changes. Extensive experiments on three different fast-slow system pairs and irregular prediction arrivals show that EvoOcc consistently improves over fast system baselines while maintaining much lower latency than the slow system, indicating a favorable accuracy-latency balance and stable behavior under practical inference situations.

title: User Attributes and Political Ideology Shape LLM Receptiveness in Online Political Debates
summary:
Online political discussions increasingly involve AI-mediated participation, as users invoke LLMs to assess contested claims, arbitrate disputes, and respond to opposing viewpoints. As these systems become participants in online exchanges, they may alter which speakers and argumentative strategies receive validation within the discussion.
  We study this interactional dimension by reconstructing 5,376 Debate.org debates as LLM conversations and running nearly 150,000 controlled multi-turn conversations that vary user political orientation, expertise, rhetorical strategy, and defended position, including conversations with competing users.
  Across naturalistic and controlled debates, we find that LLMs are systematically more receptive to left-leaning than right-leaning users. The asymmetry persists when users with different political orientations defend the same position and when opposing users appear in the same conversation, indicating that it is not fully explained by stance agreement or simple accommodation to the current speaker. Repeated interaction increases receptiveness without eliminating this ordering; expertise also matters, while rhetorical differences are smaller. The pattern appears across multiple models, but is not fixed: fine-tuning on different political corpora can largely erase or reverse it. These results show that LLMs can respond systematically differently to participants in the same political debate, making such interactional asymmetries important for understanding their emerging role in online public discourse.

title: SemaNorm: Stain Normalization via Semantic and Morphology Alignment for Robust Cross-Hospital Computational Pathology
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM) 2026
summary: Stain variability remains a major source of domain shift in computational pathology, yet existing normalization methods largely optimize color consistency without explicitly preserving morphology or diagnostic semantics. We propose SemaNorm, a self-supervised stain canonicalization stain normalizer to recover clean patches from strongly perturbed inputs, avoiding paired transfer, adversarial instability, and identity collapse. It further combines a frozen pathology foundation-model consistency loss with a differentiable nuclei-structure loss to preserve semantic and cellular organization. SemaNorm is evaluated across Camelyon17-WILDS and NCT-CRC-HE-100K using cross-hospital tumor classification, cell-graph morphology metrics, and semantic stability measured with an independent held-out foundation encoder. SemaNorm improves out-of-distribution accuracy by 5.9% over the strongest normalization baseline and by 13.5% over no normalization, while achieving the best morphology preservation. Independent foundation-model and cell-graph analyses further confirm improved semantic and structural stability. These results establish morphology- and semantics-aware optimization as a principled alternative to color-only stain normalization.

title: QFacePlacement: From Arbitrary Tensorization to Semantic Spatial Correspondence in Modern Face Verification
comment: Accepted at 11th International Conference on Computer Vision & Image Processing (CVIP)
summary: Quantum-inspired computer vision often reshapes high-dimensional features into tensors and applies tensor-network models. In face verification, this can be misleading: modern embeddings are optimized for cosine similarity, and tensorization alone does not establish the low-rank structure needed for tensor trains or matrix-product operators (MPOs). We study model placement through two controlled interfaces. First, cross-model embedding alignment requires a 512 x 512 operator to map AdaFace embeddings into ArcFace space. Dense Ridge and Procrustes mappings remain strong, while deterministic TT-SVD and MPO compression underperform even with basis changes and low-rank residuals. At a 64K-parameter storage budget, mean directional AUC is 0.9297 for dense Ridge, 0.8952 for rank-64 SVD, 0.8685 for the best low-rank-MPO hybrid, and approximately 0.649 for raw MPO. Second, before global pooling, we construct a 7 x 7 x 7 x 7 probe-gallery correspondence tensor from local AdaFace descriptors. A geometry-aware symmetric tensor train with bond dimension 2 uses 122 trainable parameters, compared with 2,403 for a dense linear matcher, while attaining an LFW AUC of 0.9802. Yet compression does not translate into better low-false-acceptance performance: on CFP-FP, TAR at FAR = 0.001 is 0.0102 versus 0.1734 for global cosine matching, and on CPLFW it is 0.7805 versus 0.8737. These results suggest that quantum-inspired factorization is most credible when the chosen interface provides task-aligned axes and compressible structure. They also show why aggregate AUC must be assessed alongside operational low-FAR metrics.

title: Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents
summary: Language model agents increasingly act on users' behalf by manipulating external environments through tools, often from high-level instructions that leave critical task- and environment-specific context unstated. To prevent resulting misaligned actions, recent work verifies proposed actions before execution, largely by establishing whether the conditions supporting them hold. We argue that this confirmation-oriented view leaves a fundamental blind spot: a wrong action often passes every check that asks whether it is right. This motivates a different question for verification: rather than asking what evidence supports an action, can the agent find evidence that refutes it? We pursue this direction with BlackSwan, a refutation-oriented, expect-suspect-test procedure that predicts the intended effect of each state-mutating action, formulates specific and empirically testable hypotheses for how it could be wrong, and tests them using existing observations or additional non-mutating actions, executing the action only if none survives testing. On challenging AppWorld tasks, BlackSwan improves success rate over the strongest baseline by 14.9 and 25.2%p with and without the backbone model's thinking mode, respectively. Even without thinking or in-context demonstrations, it outperforms stronger baselines equipped with them. The gains also transfer beyond AppWorld, with BlackSwan improving WebShop performance by 12.7%p. More broadly, our results suggest that language model agents have an underused capacity to recognize and self-correct misaligned actions, which can be systematically elicited through active conjecture and refutation before execution.

title: Memorix: Managing Memory Selections for AI Agents
summary:
AI agents now handle a growing share of tasks across sessions within a persistent project. Their behavior depends not only on the model, but heavily on the persistent state they read from the environment. Existing systems assemble this memory at use time, splicing selected files into the prompt as a one-off payload. As a result, per-task assembly is costly and can still miss critical material, failures cannot be traced or replayed, and agents can read documentation written for the wrong version. Our key insight is that what an agent should read is mostly determined by its project, so the selection can be computed once, ahead of time, and reused across tasks.
  We propose Memorix, an agent memory system that realizes this insight. Memorix achieves this via three key mechanisms: (1) an immutable and versioned Store pins every source by identity and reproduces historical layouts cheaply, (2) a View that splits selection (Derivations) from composition (Environment), making the result reproducible and shareable, and (3) Quests and Profiles keep a delivered view refreshable and available inside the project as sources evolve. We implement Memorix and evaluate it on SWE-ContextBench and LibEvolutionEval against mainstream agent memory systems. Precomputed Environments raise resolved rate by up to 1.5X and deliver the correct library version on every version-conditioned task, while cutting amortized cost by up to 100X and build time by up to 38X.

title: CellPlex: Benchmarking Single-Cell Spatial Proteomics Prediction from H&E
summary: Spatial proteomics measures tens of proteins in every cell of a tissue section, but its cost confines it to small research cohorts, whereas hematoxylin and eosin (H\&E) slides exist for nearly every patient. Inferring single-cell spatial proteomics from H\&E would bring its analyses to routine pathology, and a growing number of virtual staining models pursue this goal. Each is evaluated on its own cohort, panel and pixel-level metric, and released models transfer poorly to new cohorts, leaving open which approach to build on and which proteins H\&E can reveal. We introduce CellPlex, a benchmark that poses the task at the level of the cell: seven cohorts with same-section H\&E and multiplexed immunofluorescence, from colorectal and breast cancer to lymph-node metastases, bone marrow and glioma, with 717 samples, 44.8 million cells and 149 proteins, processed by one pipeline into per-cell targets. Pathology foundation models (PFMs) are adapted with one cell-level protocol, specialist models are fine-tuned under a matched budget, and all are scored on the same cells. Adapted PFMs are the most accurate models on every cohort, ahead of the specialists even after fine-tuning, but keep less than half of their accuracy on cohorts they were not trained on. Which proteins can be predicted depends on the tissue, not on how many cells were measured for them. By fixing the cells, targets and splits on which predictions are judged, CellPlex sets a common standard for inferring costly molecular measurements from routine H\&E and shows how far H\&E can stand in for spatial proteomics. We will release the data, splits, evaluation code and baselines as a testbed for developing and comparing future pathology foundation models and virtual staining methods.

title: Specification-Aware Predictive Uncertainty Decomposition
summary: Classical decompositions of predictive uncertainty, such as the information-theoretic one, are defined for a fixed representation $x$ of the input object. They do not consider that $x$ may be incomplete, nor do they measure how much the missing information can affect the prediction.
